"arXiv:2611.09382v1 [https://t.co/gQRNwvACTl] 06 Nov 2026
1]Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory 2]Tongji University 3]Fudan UniversityExploring Weight-Space Programming: Capabilities, Generalization, and Limitations
Junru HuCheng TangWei LiHongze ZhuChun-Mei FengQi ZhangYirong ChenMing Hu[[[Abstract
Weight-Space Programming (WSP) enables reasoning agents to directly inspect and modify neural network parameters, offering an alternative to gradient-based model adaptation. However, its capabilities, cross-task generalization, and practical limitations remain insufficiently understood. We systematically investigate WSP through 16 editing trajectories across seven benchmarks and two model scales (Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B). Our findings reveal three key insights. First, WSP can achieve substantial performance gains through highly localized interventions. On full held-out evaluations, accuracy improves by up to 29.45, 4.42, 36.72, and 17.11 percentage points on MATH-500, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, respectively. Notably, modifying only 1,023 parameters yields a 29.45-point improvement. Second, WSP exhibits promising but uneven cross-task generalization. A Math-edited checkpoint improves GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench by 3.03, 12.18, and 20.10 points, respectively, without further editing, while leaving SciCode performance unchanged. Third, effective editing remains challenging and inconsistent. Outcomes vary substantially across trajectories, and six of the 16 trajectories retain the original weights when candidate improvements cannot be reliably validated. Together, these results highlight WSP’s potential for highly localized model adaptation while revealing important challenges in intervention discovery, reliability, and cross-task transfer.Homepage: https://t.co/GBqbtgRNZF
GitHub: https://t.co/3DOVxQy7Q4 1: Overview of held-out performance following task-specific weight-space interventions.

1Introduction
Adapting pretrained neural networks typically relies on optimizing model parameters using task-specific data, as exemplified by parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods such as LoRA [3]. Prior work has also demonstrated that model behavior can be altered through direct weight interventions, including knowledge editing [6, 7] and task-vector arithmetic [4]. Recently, Weight-Space Programming (WSP) has introduced a different approach to model adaptation, enabling reasoning agents to inspect, interpret, and directly modify neural network parameters [10]. Rather than relying on gradient-based optimization or predefined editing procedures, WSP allows agents to diagnose model behavior, identify candidate computational mechanisms, and construct targeted weight modifications. This offers a promising direction for adapting pretrained models without conventional fine-tuning, potentially reducing the dependence on large task-specific training datasets while enabling more deliberate interventions in the weight space.Early results demonstrate the potential of this approach. In the original WSP study, GPT-6 Astra improves the MATH-500 accuracy of Qwen3.5-0.8B from 7.9% to 48.1% by modifying only approximately 0.016% of its parameters, primarily addressing reasoning loops that prevent the model from completing its responses [10]. The resulting improvements also extend to instruction following, suggesting that localized interventions can affect behavior beyond their original target. However, the same study reports limited success when attempting to improve a model without such identifiable failure modes. These observations raise a fundamental question:To what extent can reasoning-driven weight interventions serve as a general approach to model adaptation, rather than a means of repairing specific behavioral failures? Despite these promising initial results, the effectiveness of WSP across diverse tasks, model scales, and independently executed editing processes remains insufficiently https://t.co/K1x82N0kA6 address this question, we investigate WSP along three complementary dimensions. Capabilities: How effectively can WSP improve different model abilities, and how do the structure and scale of weight interventions relate to their outcomes? Generalization: Do improvements obtained through task-specific editing transfer to other capabilities without additional modifications, or do their effects remain confined to the target task? Limitations: How reliably can agents discover, validate, and select effective interventions, and how do editing outcomes vary across trajectories and model scales? These questions are particularly important because successful local modifications do not necessarily imply broader behavioral improvements, as also observed in prior studies of model editing and generalization [14].In this work, we conduct a systematic empirical investigation of WSP through 16 editing trajectories on Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B, covering seven benchmark families: MATH-500, MMLU-Pro, IFEval, GPQA Diamond, MedXpertQA, SciBench, and SciCode [2, 13, 15, 9, 16, 12, 11]. Our results reveal both the potential and the practical challenges of WSP. On full held-out evaluations, successful interventions achieve substantial improvements across multiple tasks, including a 29.45-percentage-point gain on MATH-500 from modifying only 1,023 parameter values. We further find that a Math-edited checkpoint transfers to GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, improving accuracy by 3.03, 12.18, and 20.10 percentage points, respectively, without further editing. However, intervention structures and outcomes vary considerably across trajectories, and six of the 16 trajectories ultimately retain the original weights when candidate improvements cannot be reliably validated. Together, these findings demonstrate that WSP can enable powerful and highly localized model adaptation, while highlighting the challenges of reliably discovering effective interventions and predicting their effects across tasks. As shown in Figure 1, WSP yield substantial held-out improvements across multiple benchmarks, particularly for the 0.8B model, while gains at the 9B scale are generally more modest.
2Methods

Pipeline Overview.
We study Weight-Space Programming (WSP) as a reasoning-driven approach to model adaptation, following the framework of [10]. As illustrated in Figure 2, GPT-6 Astra serves as the editing agent, performing targeted weight-space interventions on Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B [8]. The agent operates through a persistent Python environment for weight analysis and modification, while model inference is performed by a separate GPU worker. The original checkpoint remains unchanged throughout the editing process. Each search is allocated 50 successful forward-tool requests, enabling the agent to iteratively investigate model behavior, construct interventions, and evaluate candidate edits without access to gradients or backpropagation.Figure 2: Overview of the WSP pipeline. A reasoning agent analyzes model parameters, constructs weight interventions, and evaluates their effects using generation and teacher-forced observations. The selected checkpoint is subsequently evaluated against the original model on held-out data.

Weight-Space Editing.
Let θ0 denote the original model parameters and θt the current edited parameters. At iteration t, the agent constructs an update Δ​θt based on the current weights and accumulated observations ℋt:θt+1=bf16⁡(θt+Δ​θt),Δ​θt=Et​(θt,ℋt),(1)where Et denotes the agent-generated editing program. Updates are computed in float32 and stored in bfloat16. Edits are restricted to admissible transformer-block parameters, while token embeddings, final normalization, the language-model head, and the model architecture remain fixed. The agent may construct arbitrary interventions within these constraints, including sparse MLP modifications, rank-one updates, attention-head rescaling, and combinations of these operations. All updates are computed directly from weights and observations rather than gradient-based optimization.
Feedback and Evaluation.
The agent evaluates candidate edits through two complementary modes: autoregressive generation, which measures task performance, and teacher forcing, which provides token log-probabilities and intermediate activations for mechanistic analysis. Based on development feedback, the agent selects a final checkpoint, which is subsequently evaluated against the original model on held-out benchmarks under matched evaluation settings.
3Experiments

3.1Benchmarks and Experimental Setup
We evaluate WSP on seven benchmarks covering math reasoning (MATH [2]), general knowledge (MMLU-Pro [13]), instruction following (IFEval [15]), scientific QA (GPQA Diamond [9]), medical QA (MedXpertQA [16]), scientific reasoning (SciBench [12]), and scientific coding (SciCode [11]). We study Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B, reporting one editing trajectory for each model–benchmark pair. For 0.8B MATH, the main tables report the column-507 editing trajectory; two further trajectories are analyzed separately. Each search begins from the original checkpoint and allows up to 50 forward-tool requests for generation and teacher-forced analysis. The agent selects its final checkpoint using development feedback alone, with the option of retaining the original weights.Evaluation follows benchmark-specific protocols. IFEval uses a fixed 270/271 split of its 541 official prompts. SciBench employs numerical answer extraction with a 5% relative tolerance, while SciCode evaluates complete executable code chains, separately from the conditional unit tests used during development. Further evaluation details are provided in the appendix.
3.2Experimental Results

Development and Held-out Performance.
Table 2 summarizes the development and held-out results across 14 representative WSP editing trajectories, covering seven benchmarks and two model scales. For 0.8B Math, we report the single-column editing trajectory, with two additional independent searches analyzed separately.Across all seven benchmark categories, Qwen3.5-0.8B exhibits larger best-observed development gains than Qwen3.5-9B, with improvements reaching +43.75 percentage points on both Math and IFEval. On held-out evaluations, the 0.8B model achieves gains of +29.45, +4.42, +36.72, and +17.11 points on Math, GPQA Diamond, IFEval, and SciBench, respectively. The 9B model also improves on IFEval, SciBench, and SciCode, although with smaller gains.However, development improvements do not always translate into retained edits. In six trajectories, Astra ultimately selects the original checkpoint. Notably, the evaluated 9B Math candidate decreases held-out accuracy by 0.35 points, despite a +29.69-point development gain. These results highlight the distinction between candidate discovery, held-out performance, and final checkpoint selection.

3.3Exploration Trajectory
Figure 3 shows the complete 50-request exploration trajectory of the 0.8B MATH experiment, comprising 32 generation requests and 18 teacher-forced analyses. The agent progresses from behavioral diagnosis and component exploration to targeted interventions, controls, and broader validation. The trajectory illustrates how iterative feedback guides intervention discovery and selection.Figure 3: Exploration of the 0.8B MATH edit over 50 requests: development accuracy (top) and feedback modes (bottom).

3.4Analysis of Weight-Space Interventions

Weight-Space Interventions Generalize to Unseen Questions.
Our results demonstrate that weight-space interventions can improve performance on previously unseen questions. Across three independent Math editing trajectories, Qwen3.5-0.8B achieves held-out gains of +29.45, +5.00, and +27.30 percentage points. Task-specific edits also improve GPQA Diamond (+4.42 pp), IFEval (+36.72 pp), and SciBench (+17.11 pp) on complete held-out evaluations (Table 2). Together, these results establish that WSP improvements can extend beyond the development data used to construct the interventions.
Editing Outcomes Vary Across Independent Searches.
The three independent MATH searches exhibit substantial variation in their discovered interventions and held-out performance (Figure 4). Despite targeting the same model and benchmark, the primary search achieves a +29.45 percentage-point improvement, while reruns 1 and 2 yield gains of +5.00 and +27.30 points, respectively. Although all three interventions modify the layer-23 MLP down-projection, they differ considerably in structure and parameter support. These results highlight the path-dependent nature of weight-space exploration, where different search trajectories can discover markedly different solutions within the same model.Figure 4: Three MATH searches yield distinct interventions and different held-out improvements on the same model.

Intervention Structure Matters Beyond Scale.
Figure 5 reveals a striking contrast among three Math editing trajectories. Although all three interventions target the layer-23 MLP down-projection, they occupy three distinct regions of the parameter-scale–performance space. The primary run modifies only 1,023 BF16 values in a single output column, achieving the largest held-out improvement of +29.45 percentage points. In contrast, rerun 1 modifies 1,037,572 values through a rank-one update but yields only +5.00 points, while rerun 2 changes 1,981,083 values and achieves +27.30 points. These contrasting outcomes demonstrate that the number of modified parameters alone does not predict editing effectiveness. Rather, intervention structure and the selection of computational targets play critical roles in determining downstream performance.Figure 5: Parameter support, edit structure, and held-out gain across three layer-23 MLP interventions.

Weight-Space Interventions Exhibit Cross-Task Transfer.
To investigate cross-task generalization, we evaluate four task-edited checkpoints across additional benchmarks without further weight modifications, as shown in Figure 6. On Qwen3.5-0.8B, the Math-edited checkpoint achieves 28.28% on GPQA Diamond, 33.58% on IFEval, and 21.48% on SciBench. Conversely, the IFEval-edited checkpoint improves performance on Math and SciBench, reaching 21.40% and 3.28%, respectively. Cross-task effects are also observed at the 9B scale: the IFEval-edited checkpoint achieves 75.71% on SciBench, while the SciBench-edited checkpoint reaches 91.51% on IFEval. However, transfer is not uniformly beneficial, with some interventions producing marginal improvements or performance regressions on other tasks. These results demonstrate that weight-space interventions can influence capabilities beyond their original objectives, while the direction and magnitude of transfer depend on both the source intervention and the target task.

Figure 6: Cross-task transfer of four task-edited checkpoints: 0.8B Math and IFEval (A–B), and 9B IFEval and SciBench (C–D). Dashed gray lines denote the base model; blue lines denote the transferred edited checkpoint.

Limited Search Budgets Constrain Weight Editing.
Within the 50-request budget, Astra does not always identify a sufficiently reliable weight intervention. For example, in 0.8B MedXpertQA, 9B GPQA Diamond, 9B MedXpertQA, and 9B MMLU-Pro, the agent ultimately retains the original weights despite observing positive development gains. For instance, the 9B GPQA search achieves an initial improvement of +6.25 percentage points, but subsequent validation shows a slight performance decline. Similarly, the 9B MMLU-Pro search identifies promising candidates whose improvements diminish under broader evaluation. These outcomes highlight a practical limitation of WSP: within a fixed exploration budget, the agent may fail to discover and validate an intervention sufficiently effective to justify modifying the original model.
Model Scale and Baseline Headroom Shape Editing Outcomes.
Figure 7 reveals a consistent contrast between baseline capability and observed editing gains across model scales. Qwen3.5-9B substantially outperforms Qwen3.5-0.8B before editing, particularly on MATH-500 (97.70% versus 8.35%) and SciBench (72.46% versus 1.38%). In contrast, the 0.8B model achieves larger best-observed development gains across all seven benchmark categories. This pattern highlights the role of initial model capability and available improvement headroom in weight-space editing. The results suggest that smaller models offer greater opportunities for measurable improvements, while stronger models present a more constrained search landscape.Figure 7: Baseline accuracy and best-observed development gains for Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-9B.

4Discussion
Our systematic evaluation reveals both the potential and limitations of Weight-Space Programming. Across diverse tasks and model scales, WSP achieves substantial held-out improvements and exhibits asymmetric cross-task transfer, with both beneficial and adverse effects. Independent editing trajectories further show that effectiveness depends not only on the number of modified parameters, but also on intervention structure, computational targets, and exploration paths. However, development gains do not always translate into reliable held-out improvements, and repeated evaluations incur substantial computational costs. The mechanisms governing successful editing and generalization remain unclear, including the effects of jointly modifying multiple parameter locations and the influence of development data size and diversity. Moreover, WSP has yet to be systematically evaluated on longer-horizon reasoning and complex agentic tasks. These findings highlight the need for more reliable intervention selection, efficient evaluation, and deeper mechanistic understanding.

5Supplementary Experimental Protocol
Each search pairs an editor model, GPT-6 Astra at maximum reasoning effort, with a target model, Qwen3.5-0.8B or Qwen3.5-9B. The editor observes the target only through forward requests, with a budget of 50 successful requests per search. It may also run up to 300 Python analyses per search to inspect weights, analyze returned observations, and compute edits. These analyses do not run inference on the target model.There are two request types, and each successful request of either type counts once against the budget. A generation request (G) samples answers from the target and returns them with task scores when the items come from a graded set. A teacher-forced request (TF) scores continuations supplied by the editor, returning conditional log-probabilities and any requested activations. TF requests yield no task accuracy. The editor chooses the questions, batch size, number of samples, token cap, and weight states for each request, and it may adapt these choices to earlier observations. One request can therefore contain many prompts and samples, as well as both the original and the edited weights..."

results.input: Giải giúp mình bài toán tích phân: nguyên hàm của x^2 là gì?

result.actual_text:
Nguyên hàm của hàm số \( x^2 \) được tính bằng cách sử dụng quy tắc tích phân cơ bản. Cụ thể, nguyên hàm của \( x^n \) (với \( n \neq -1 \)) là:

\[
\int x^n \, dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C
\]

Trong trường hợp này, với \( n = 2 \):

\[
\int x^2 \, dx = \frac{x^{2+1}}{2+1} + C = \frac{x^3}{3} + C
\]

Vậy nguyên hàm của \( x^2 \) là:

\[
\frac{x^3}{3} + C
\]

Trong đó \( C \) là hằng số tích phân.

items.summary:
老美要封杀光模块，微软第一个不答应
今天看到一条挺有意思的新闻。
川子哥又准备对中国科技产业动刀了，这次盯上的依旧是光模块。
但这次有意思的地方在于，按理说美国要封杀中国企业，最着急的应该是国内小伙伴，结果我们这边还没怎么吭声，微软先跳出来反对了。
根据今天某透的独家报道，特朗普政府正在考虑禁止新型号的中国光模块进入美国市场，而微软正在游说美国政府，希望他们放弃这个计划。
先做个声明，本文仅作产业讨论，并非也不构成任何投资建议
海外云厂商在未来的几年里是无法拒绝中国光模块的我在之前也说过，但是并不代表相关企业就没有风险，因为本质是预期
那么这次微软也不是良心发现，他也没那么好心，核心是怕把中国光模块禁了，耽误了自己的数据中心进度
毕竟目前的中国企业供应了全球大约三分之二的光模块
另一方面，根据报道，微软目前在美国有35座数据中心正在建设，还有134座处于规划阶段。
而现在一个大型AI数据中心，可能需要数十万甚至数百万只光模块。
所以，如果一旦立马禁了，这些嗷嗷待哺的牛批已经吹出去，写到了下季度下年度预期中的数据中心建设谁来负责呢？
我之前讲过的COHR和LITE虽然很厉害，但还是主要在上游的激光器、光芯片这些领域
在大规模制造的下游光模块业务中，美国相关供应商是不太可能在未来12—24个月内完全承接我们这边的出货规模的。
所以，我之前在讲电赛道里也提到，当前对于传统ai硬件来说
比如gpu，最尴尬的是下游数据中心建设，比如微软花了几十亿美元买回来一大堆英伟达的GPU，结果数据中心的电，光没办法按时交付，那整个项目就可能因此延期。
因此造成的延误倒还可以估量，但是因此造成的gpu等硬件随着时间而产生的技术落后是无法估量的
以前我在讲电的时候，反复强调过一个观点。
对于那些正在疯狂建设数据中心的科技巨头来说，他们购买的很多东西，表面上看是电力、设备、基础设施，但实际上购买的是时间。
而时间这个简单的词就是当下数据中心和ai研发者支付远高于传统芯片制造业溢价的核心所在
本质是在今天的AI竞赛中，提前半年把数据中心建起来，比在设备采购上节省几个十几个百分点的成本重要得多。这块也是马斯克在周末讲解spacex明年展望时重点提到的
当然了，今天的光模块不危险，不代表几年后不危险。
我之前也提到美国势必利用未来几年的窗口期，逐渐建立起一套能够替代中国供应商的产能体系，尤其是到了3.2T甚至更远的下一代产品，光赛道的竞争格局，是可能发生变化的。
今天这个消息不是简单用利好或者利空来概括。
微软也不是什么好心人，只不过为了自己的商业利益，为现有供应链争取继续合作的空间。
但长期看，美国想降低对他国ai硬件的依赖，这个方向是不会轻易改变的。

items.title: OpenAI can now cut off any of its research AI jobs within 35 seconds, even if the job's own code tries to keep going.
items.summary:
OpenAI can now cut off any of its research AI jobs within 35 seconds, even if the job's own code tries to keep going.

it's called Control Room (announced Nov 9). per OpenAI's post, as reported by Interesting Engineering and RuntimeWire:
- every research job gets a unique ID that rides along on each model request
- before answering, the inference engine checks: is this job still authorized?
- stopped job = no more model outputs, even if the script keeps running
- fail-closed: if Control Room itself goes down or is tampered with, engines refuse requests
- covers RL experiments, evals and big data-processing jobs. ChatGPT and the API have their own takedown systems
- 35s is the max delay, caused by an authorization cache. OpenAI says it's working to cut it to zero
- a separate model-based monitor watches frontier RL jobs and can trigger the stop

the lesson if you run agents: put the off switch where the model calls go (your gateway or proxy), not inside the agent's own code. and decide now what happens when the switch itself breaks.
